hints: Focus on getting every quantity into the correct SI units before you touch the ideal gas equation.
Convert 60 degrees C to kelvin and 103 kPa to pascals, then rearrange to n = pV / RT to find moles of methane.
Multiply your moles by the molar mass of methane, 16.0 g mol-1, and round to two significant figures to get the mass in grams.
walkthrough:
**Convert to SI units**

Great start, let's get our units ready. The gas constant R = 8.31 needs pressure in Pa, volume in m3 and temperature in K.

$$T = 60 + 273 = 333 \text{ K}$$
$$p = 103 \text{ kPa} = 103 \times 1000 = 103000 \text{ Pa}$$
$$V = 5.37 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$$

**Use pV = nRT to find moles**

Now rearrange the ideal gas equation to find n. This tells us how much methane we actually have.

$$n = \frac{pV}{RT} = \frac{103000 \times 5.37 \times 10^{-3}}{8.31 \times 333}$$
$$n = \frac{553.11}{2767.23} \approx 0.20 \text{ mol}$$

**Convert moles to mass**

Finally, turn moles into grams using the molar mass of methane, $\text{CH}_4$.

$$M_r(\text{CH}_4) = 12.0 + (4 \times 1.0) = 16.0 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$$
$$m = n \times M_r = 0.20 \times 16.0 \approx 3.2 \text{ g}$$

options.A: Incorrect. This uses pressure in kPa instead of Pa. You get n about 1000 times too small, giving 0.0032 g. Always multiply kPa by 1000 to get Pa when R = 8.31.
options.B: Incorrect. This makes two unit errors at once, using kPa for pressure and degrees C for temperature. That gives a tiny mole value and 0.018 g. Convert p to Pa and T to K first.
options.C: Correct. With p = 103000 Pa, V = 5.37 x 10-3 m3 and T = 333 K, n = pV/RT is about 0.20 mol. Times 16.0 g mol-1 for methane gives 3.2 g to two significant figures.
options.D: Incorrect. This uses temperature as 60 degrees C instead of 333 K. A much smaller T on the bottom makes n much too large, giving about 18 g. Always add 273 to convert to kelvin.
